newsitem.title: MEXICO: Cargill crusher seen aiding Mexico efficiency.
newsitem.headline: Cargill crusher seen aiding Mexico efficiency.

text.p: A new Cargill Inc soybean crusher scheduled to open February 3 in Tula, Hidalgo state, will test the efficiency of Mexican competitors, the American Soybean Association (ASA) said in a report obtained on Monday by Reuters.
Cargill, the world's largest privately held company, is expected to process 1,500 tonnes of mainly U.S.-grown soybeans per day for the Mexican market, the company said last week in a news release.

"This brings us to the conclusion that the oil crushing industry, much like the poultry industry, will consolidate more and more in Mexico," the report said. "The added competition is expected to force more efficiency into the entire industry."
The ASA estimated Cargill's annual Mexican crush at 520,000 tonnes and said the plant's facility could double its volume by its second year of operation.
The ASA report also said Cargill will use its own rail cars, leading to lower transport costs.

A company representative told Reuters that soybeans will "not exclusively" be transported through Nuevo Laredo in Mexico and Laredo, Texas, where most competitors buy, and that beans and soy products will be transported by rail and sea. He would not comment on transportation costs.
The ASA report also said the central location of Tula will be an advantage for Cargill because of lower transportation costs from Hidalgo to the neighboring major consumption center of Mexico City.
Mexican crushers are mainly located further away, near the U.S. border or in southeastern Mexico.
The ASA said it expected plants in Sonora and Sinaloa states would soon shut their doors.
"Depending on the success of the new Cargill plant, the closing date for those crushers in northwest will probably be accelerated," the report said.
Closures will not likely indicate fewer soybeans processed, the report said, and vegetable oil production may increase as an improving economy spurs increased consumption.

"What we can expect as some smaller crushing companies cease operations and the new Cargill plant comes on stream is more shipments of grain in unit trains and boatloads and less shipments in small orders. This will make border crossings more fluid as it is easier to cross a unit train that one car load at a time," the report said.
